questionText: Listen to an academic advisor explaining graduation requirements to second-year students.
audioScript:
Situation: An academic advisor addresses a group of second-year undergraduates at a graduation requirements information session.
Advisor: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Dr. Helen Whittaker, your academic advisor. Today I'll walk you through the requirements you must meet to graduate from Crestfield University.
Advisor: First, every undergraduate must complete one hundred and twenty credits in total. Of these, forty-five must come from your major subjects, and thirty from general education modules.
Student: Excuse me, is there a minimum grade we need to pass a module?
Advisor: Yes. You must achieve at least a D, which is fifty percent, to earn credit for any module. Anything below that and you'll have to retake it.
Student: Do we need to do a final year project?
Advisor: Indeed. All students must complete a dissertation worth fifteen credits in their final year. You'll choose your topic in the first semester and submit it by the end of April.
Advisor: Additionally, there's a community engagement requirement. You must log at least twenty hours of approved volunteer work before graduation.
Student: What happens if we don't meet the volunteer hours?
Advisor: Without those hours, your degree will be withheld until the requirement is fulfilled, even if all your credits are complete.
Advisor: Lastly, all students must pass a quantitative reasoning exam, which is held each November. You have two attempts. If you fail both, you'll need to take a remedial course over the summer.

questionText: Listen to a recreation coordinator describing campus recreation facilities to new students.
audioScript:
Situation: A campus recreation coordinator welcomes new students and explains the recreational facilities and programmes available at the university.
Coordinator: Hi everyone, I'm Marcus, the campus recreation coordinator here at Lakeside University. Let me tell you about what's on offer for staying active and having fun.
Coordinator: Our main sports complex, the Allen Centre, has a twenty-five-metre swimming pool, six badminton courts, and a fully equipped gym. It's open from six in the morning until eleven at night, seven days a week.
Student: Do we have to pay to use the gym?
Coordinator: Good news, no. Gym access is included in your student fees, so just swipe your ID card at the entrance. However, fitness classes like yoga and spin cost three pounds per session.
Student: Can we book courts in advance?
Coordinator: Absolutely. You can reserve badminton and squash courts online up to a week ahead. Each booking is limited to one hour so that everyone gets a fair turn.
Coordinator: We also run intramural leagues in football, basketball, and netball. Sign-ups close at the end of the second week of term, and matches are played on Wednesday afternoons.
Student: Are there any outdoor facilities?
Coordinator: Yes, we have three floodlit tennis courts and a running track behind the Allen Centre. The track is open round the clock, but the tennis courts close at nine in the evening to keep noise down for nearby residents.
Coordinator: Finally, we organise weekend hiking trips once a month. Tickets are five pounds and include transport. They sell out fast, so book early at the recreation office.

questionText: Listen to a volunteer coordinator describing opportunities at a volunteer fair.
audioScript:
Situation: A volunteer coordinator from the student community office addresses students at a volunteer opportunities fair, outlining various placements available this semester.
Coordinator: Welcome, everyone. I'm Sarah Cheng, the volunteer coordinator at Northgate University. Today I'll introduce four fantastic volunteer programmes you can join this semester.
Coordinator: First is the Reading Partners scheme. You'll spend two hours each week helping primary school children with their reading. It takes place at Greenfield Primary, a short bus ride from campus, on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.
Student: Do we need any experience for that?
Coordinator: No prior experience is needed. You'll receive a one-hour training session before you start. And here's the reward: volunteers who complete a full term with Reading Partners earn both a certificate of achievement and a reference letter, which is brilliant for your CV.
Coordinator: Second is the Elderly Companions programme. Volunteers visit seniors at the Sunnybank Care Home. You'll chat, play games, and sometimes help with light shopping. A background check is required, which the university covers at no cost to you.
Student: How long is the commitment for that one?
Coordinator: We ask for a minimum of one semester, so about twelve weeks, to build meaningful relationships with the residents.
Coordinator: Third is the Community Garden Group. It meets every Saturday morning from nine to noon at the campus allotment. You'll grow vegetables that are donated to the local food bank. Tools and seeds are provided, but you should bring your own gloves.
Coordinator: Finally, the Beach Clean-Up Initiative takes place at Seaton Beach, about twenty minutes by coach. It runs once a month, usually on the last Sunday. The university provides gloves, bags, and transport. Last year, volunteers collected over three hundred kilograms of litter.
Coordinator: All volunteers who log more than thirty hours across any combination of programmes also receive a special commendation from the vice-chancellor.

questionText: Listen to a housing officer presenting student accommodation options to incoming students.
audioScript:
Situation: A university housing officer presents on-campus and off-campus housing options to a group of incoming students at an accommodation briefing.
Officer: Welcome, everyone. I'm Sarah, the student housing officer at Brookfield University. Today I'll outline your accommodation options so you can make an informed choice.
Officer: First, we have three on-campus residence halls. Maple Court is the most affordable at ninety pounds per week, but it's a shared twin room with a communal kitchen. Oak House offers single rooms with a shared bathroom at one hundred and twenty pounds per week.
Student: Are meals included in any of the halls?
Officer: Yes, in Cedar Lodge, our premium option, the weekly rent of one hundred and sixty pounds includes a half-board meal plan, meaning breakfast and dinner are provided on weekdays.
Student: What about private rented housing off campus?
Officer: Many second and third-year students rent flats in the nearby area. A typical one-bedroom flat costs around five hundred pounds per month, plus bills. The university keeps an approved landlord list on the housing portal to help you avoid problems.
Student: Is there a homestay option for international students?
Officer: Indeed. We partner with local families who host students for one hundred and fifty pounds per week, which includes a private room and all meals. It's a great way to improve your English.
Officer: Whichever option you choose, you must submit your housing application by the fifteenth of August. Late applications are placed on a waiting list and only considered if spaces open up.
Officer: A deposit of two hundred pounds is required to secure your place, and it's refundable at the end of your tenancy provided there's no damage.

questionText: Listen to a campus security supervisor briefing staff on patrol procedures.
audioScript:
Situation: A campus security supervisor briefs a team of new patrol officers on procedures and protocols at the start of their shift.
Supervisor: Right, listen up. I'm Officer Daniels, your shift supervisor. This briefing covers our patrol procedures for the night shift, so pay close attention.
Supervisor: Our patrol route covers three zones. Zone A is the academic block, Zone B is the residential halls, and Zone C is the sports and recreation area. Each zone must be patrolled at least once every hour.
Officer: What should we do if we find a door that should be locked but isn't?
Supervisor: Good question. First, check whether anyone is inside. If the area is clear, secure the door and log the incident in the patrol report with the time and door number. If someone is inside, ask for their ID and verify they have authorisation.
Officer: And what's the protocol for dealing with suspicious individuals?
Supervisor: Approach calmly, identify yourself as campus security, and ask if they need assistance. If they refuse to cooperate or cannot give a reason for being on campus, call the control room immediately and do not attempt to detain them yourself.
Supervisor: For emergencies, use the code red over the radio. That triggers an immediate response from all nearby units. Code yellow means a non-urgent incident that still needs backup, like a reported theft.
Officer: What about medical emergencies?
Supervisor: For any medical situation, call an ambulance first, then radio code blue so the nearest first-aid-trained officer responds. Never move a seriously injured person unless they're in immediate danger.
Supervisor: Finally, all incidents must be written up in the logbook before the end of your shift. Reports submitted after seven in the morning are considered late and require a written explanation.

questionText: Listen to a sustainability officer leading a tour of the campus environmental initiatives.
audioScript:
Situation: A university sustainability officer leads a group of students on a tour showcasing the campus's environmental initiatives and green infrastructure.
Officer: Hello, and welcome to the Green Campus Tour. I'm Dr. Eleanor Hayes, the sustainability officer here at Westwood University. Over the next hour, I'll show you how our campus is reducing its environmental footprint.
Officer: We'll begin at the solar panel array on the roof of the science block. Installed in 2021, these panels generate fifteen per cent of the university's electricity, saving approximately two hundred tonnes of carbon emissions annually.
Student: That's impressive. Is there more renewable infrastructure?
Officer: Indeed. Next, we have the rainwater harvesting system beneath the engineering building. It collects runoff from rooftops and irrigates the campus lawns and gardens. In a typical year, the system saves around one million litres of mains water.
Student: Are there any green buildings on campus?
Officer: Yes, our new student centre, opened last spring, is a showcase. It's constructed almost entirely from locally sourced, recycled materials, including reclaimed timber and recycled steel. The design prioritises natural light and ventilation.
Officer: Over to your right, you'll notice the biodiversity garden. Its main purpose is to attract and protect native pollinators, such as bees and butterflies, by providing the right wildflowers and habitats. Student volunteers help maintain it.
Student: Is there a way to get around campus without a car?
Officer: Absolutely. We run a bicycle hire scheme. Students can register online for a free annual membership, which allows unlimited borrowing from bike stations across campus. It's proven very popular.
Officer: Our environmental policy, approved by the university senate, pledges to reduce waste sent to landfill by fifty per cent within five years. We're currently in year three and on track to meet that target.
Officer: Finally, all of this is documented in our campus sustainability report, which is published annually and available on the university website. It tracks our progress against every target I've mentioned today.

questionText: Listen to a mentorship programme coordinator introducing the student mentorship scheme to first-year students.
audioScript:
Situation: A mentorship programme coordinator introduces the university's student mentorship scheme to an audience of first-year students at an induction event.
Coordinator: Good morning, everyone. I'm Professor James Aldridge, and I coordinate the Bridges Mentorship Programme here at Thornfield University. Let me explain how it works.
Coordinator: The programme pairs each first-year student with a trained mentor from the third or fourth year. Mentors provide academic guidance, social support, and help you navigate university life during your first two semesters.
Student: How do we get matched with a mentor?
Coordinator: Great question. You'll complete an online questionnaire that asks about your course, interests, and any preferences, such as same-gender matching. Our algorithm then pairs you within forty-eight hours, and you'll receive your mentor's contact details by email.
Student: How often are we supposed to meet?
Coordinator: We ask mentors and mentees to meet face-to-face at least twice a month, for about an hour each time. You can also contact your mentor by email or message between meetings, but mentors aren't expected to reply outside working hours.
Coordinator: Mentors receive training in active listening, safeguarding, and signposting to university services. They are not counsellors, so if you're dealing with a serious issue, they'll refer you to the appropriate professional service.
Student: What if we don't get along with our mentor?
Coordinator: That does happen occasionally. You can request a reassignment through the programme portal within the first six weeks, no questions asked. After six weeks, requests are reviewed case by case.
Coordinator: At the end of the year, both mentors and mentees submit a short reflection report. Mentees who complete the programme receive a certificate that can be added to your higher education achievement report, which is useful for job applications.
Coordinator: Registration opens today and closes on the twentieth of September. There's no cost, but places are limited to three hundred mentees, so I encourage you to sign up promptly.
